elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在了解埃博拉病毒如何在中枢神经系统的免疫特权环境中建立持续感染,解决有关人类神经组织慢性感染和复发机制的知识差距。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 研究人员开发了一种人脑类器官模型来分析人类神经组织中的正埃博拉病毒感染,在长达 120 天的时间内测试了埃博拉病毒、苏丹病毒、雷斯顿病毒和马尔堡病毒。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究使用人脑类器官来研究病毒的持久性,检查病毒通过出芽和直接细胞间 传播 的传播,以及病毒 进化 和有缺陷的病毒 基因组 的积累。
elements_zh.main_results: EBOV 在多种神经细胞类型中持续存在长达 120 天,包括神经元、星形胶质细胞、小胶质细胞和少突胶质细胞,其持续存在与病毒 进化 的持续存在和缺陷病毒 基因组 的积累有关。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,埃博拉病毒利用中枢神经系统的免疫特权状态,通过细胞间传播和有缺陷的病毒 基因组 等机制建立长期持久性,为病毒适应神经环境提供了新的见解。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果强调中枢神经系统是埃博拉病毒持续存在的潜在储存宿主,这可能导致幸存者复发和慢性神经炎症,从而为监测和预防策略提供信息。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 由于对类器官模型的依赖,该模型可能无法完全复制人类中枢神经系统的复杂性,并且其他正埃博拉病毒物种的机制保守性存在不确定性,因此证据强度中等。

PHOENIX - Health officials in Arizona say they have confirmed a case of Mpox (formerly Monkeypox) that involves a different type of the same virus. What we know: In a statement released on July 22, officials with the Arizona Department of Health Services said the case involved a type of Mpox that is classified as "Clade I." They say this is the first time Arizona has seen a case of confirmed Clade I Mpox. "The individual acquired the infection while traveling outside the country," read a portion of the statement. Dig deeper: According to a factsheet published by the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, Clade I is one of two main types of Mpox. The factsheet notes identified Clade II as the one that caused an outbreak in the U.S. The factsheet states that Clade I Mpox is "more likely to cause severe illness and death, especially in people who are immunocompromised." Officials say Clade I Mpox is "mostly transmitted through exposure to animals who carry the disease," while also stating that it can be transmitted through household contexts close sexual or intimate contact, and contaminated objects (fomites). In comparison, the factsheet states that Clade II of Mpox is mostly transmitted through same-sex sexual contact. As for the mortality rate for the virus, the factsheet states it ranges from 1% to 10% for Clade I, and from less than 1% to 4% for Clade II. Local perspective: In their statement, AZDHS officials say there are 34 reported cases of Mpox in Arizona as of July 21, which includes the Clade I case. "There is currently no evidence of local transmission connected to this case," officials wrote. What you can do: The factsheet from Johns Hopkins states that two doses of the JYNNEOS vaccines are "expected to protect against both Clade I and Clade II infections." Meanwhile, Arizona health officials say people should contact their healthcare provider or the local health department as soon as possible if they wer exposed to someone with Mpox, noting that vaccination can happen after exposure. "Vaccination is most effective when given within four days of exposure but may still reduce illness when given within 14 days. Check for symptoms for 21 days after your last contact." The Source: Information for this article was gathered from a statement released by the Arizona Department of Public Health, and from a factsheet published by the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. travel-associated case of Clade I mpoxBy Mitchell KochPublished: Jul. 22, 2026 at 11:49 PM UTCShareAdd Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on GooglePHOENIX (AZFamily) — Arizona health officials announced Wednesday that they are tracking the state’s first travel-associated case of a unique mpox strain. The Arizona Department of Health Services (ADHS) said it was notified this month of a state resident who contracted Clade I mpox while traveling outside the country.ADHS and other local public health officials are now monitoring and following up with people who may have been exposed. The department added that there is no evidence of local transmission at this time related to this case. Mpox has two strains: Clade I and Clade II. The latter has been spreading in Arizona and the United States since 2022, ADHS said. Clade I is usually found in parts of Africa and is not common in the U.S., ADHS said. Both strains cause similar symptoms, and officials recommend the same treatment methods: testing, vaccination, clinical management and public health response. The department said Arizona has seen an increase in reported mpox cases this summer. As of July 21, the state had 34 reported cases — both strains included — this year. What is mpox?According to ADHS, mpox is an infection caused by the monkeypox virus. It mainly spreads through close personal contact with someone who has mpox, like the following: Direct skin-to-skin contact with a rash, sores, scabs or body fluidsClose physical contactSharing bedding, towels, clothing or other personal itemsProlonged close contact with someone who has mpoxThe infection can pass to a baby during pregnancy Casual contact in places such as stores, offices or airplanes is unlikely to spread mpoxIf exposed, symptoms may include a new or unexplained rash that looks like pimples or blisters and may be painful or itchy. Some people may also experience fever, headache, muscle aches, swollen lymph nodes, chills, exhaustion or respiratory symptoms.People with weaker immune systems may be at greater risk of severe illness from mpox. What can you do? Get vaccinated if you think you may be at risk. If you recently had close physical contact with someone who has mpox, you have an increased risk of contracting the disease. ADHS said the JYNNEOS vaccine can help prevent mpox and reduce the risk of severe illness.If you were exposed to someone with mpox, contact a healthcare provider or local health department as soon as possible. You can get vaccinated after an exposure. Vaccination is most effective when given within four days of exposure but may still reduce illness when given within 14 days. Check for symptoms for 21 days after your last contact. If you develop symptoms, avoid close contact with others, isolate at home and contact your healthcare provider for testing. Tell your provider about any recent travel and other possible exposure to mpox.See a spelling or grammatical error in our story? travel-associated case of Clade I mpoxBy Mitchell KochPublished: Jul. 22, 2026 at 11:49 PM UTCShareAdd Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on GooglePHOENIX (AZFamily) — Arizona health officials announced Wednesday that they are tracking the state’s first travel-associated case of a unique mpox strain. The Arizona Department of Health Services (ADHS) said it was notified this month of a state resident who contracted Clade I mpox while traveling outside the country.ADHS and other local public health officials are now monitoring and following up with people who may have been exposed. The department added that there is no evidence of local transmission at this time related to this case. Mpox has two strains: Clade I and Clade II. The latter has been spreading in Arizona and the United States since 2022, ADHS said. Clade I is usually found in parts of Africa and is not common in the U.S., ADHS said. Both strains cause similar symptoms, and officials recommend the same treatment methods: testing, vaccination, clinical management and public health response. The department said Arizona has seen an increase in reported mpox cases this summer. As of July 21, the state had 34 reported cases — both strains included — this year. What is mpox?According to ADHS, mpox is an infection caused by the monkeypox virus. It mainly spreads through close personal contact with someone who has mpox, like the following: Direct skin-to-skin contact with a rash, sores, scabs or body fluidsClose physical contactSharing bedding, towels, clothing or other personal itemsProlonged close contact with someone who has mpoxThe infection can pass to a baby during pregnancy Casual contact in places such as stores, offices or airplanes is unlikely to spread mpoxIf exposed, symptoms may include a new or unexplained rash that looks like pimples or blisters and may be painful or itchy. Some people may also experience fever, headache, muscle aches, swollen lymph nodes, chills, exhaustion or respiratory symptoms.People with weaker immune systems may be at greater risk of severe illness from mpox. What can you do? Get vaccinated if you think you may be at risk. If you recently had close physical contact with someone who has mpox, you have an increased risk of contracting the disease. ADHS said the JYNNEOS vaccine can help prevent mpox and reduce the risk of severe illness.If you were exposed to someone with mpox, contact a healthcare provider or local health department as soon as possible. You can get vaccinated after an exposure. Vaccination is most effective when given within four days of exposure but may still reduce illness when given within 14 days. Check for symptoms for 21 days after your last contact. If you develop symptoms, avoid close contact with others, isolate at home and contact your healthcare provider for testing. news.content: HEALTH Arizona confirms first case of deadlier mpox strain Stephanie Innes Arizona Republic July 23, 2026 Updated July 24, 2026, 9:43 a.m. MT Arizona health officials confirmed the state's first-ever case of a more lethal strain of mpox in a patient who acquired the infection while traveling outside of the United States. The Clade I strain of mpox is known to cause more serious illness and has higher death rates than the more common Clade II strain. Clade I is, to date, far more rare in the United States than Clade II mpox, which has been circulating in the country since 2022. The Arizona Department of Health Services said the risk to the general public is low and there's no evidence that Clade I mpox is spreading in Arizona. According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the risk posed by the Clade I mpox outbreak to most people remains low. The risk to men who have sex with men is low to moderate , the federal agency says. Federal health officials said that as of June 2026 there had been at least 20 Clade I mpox cases reported in the United States and that the incidence of the cases began to increase in frequency in the beginning of March 2026. Mpox, formerly known as monkeypox, is a viral infection similar to smallpox that typically causes painful rashes with sores and blisters and swollen lymph nodes and it typically spreads through skin-to-skin contact with the sores, blisters and body fluids. Other ways the virus can spread include: from infected animals; from sharing bedding, towels, clothing or other personal items; and prolonged close contact with someone who has mpox. The virus can pass to a baby during pregnancy, state health officials said, and casual contact in places such as stores, offices, or airplanes is unlikely to spread mpox. State is not providing details about the Arizona patient Citing patient privacy, the Arizona Department of Health Services would not disclose the age or gender of the person who was infected, nor would they disclose the county where the infected person resides, or if the person had been hospitalized. They also did not say whether the case was subclade Ia or Ib. The CDC as of June 2 was reporting that recent travel-associated Clade I mpox cases have almost exclusively been attributed to subclade Ib and that there have been no deaths associated with the cases. While the robust health care system in the United States has been able to treat people with Clade I mpox, globally it has proven more deadly, according to the CDC, with more than 55,000 confirmed cases since January 2024, including more than 150 deaths. As of July 21 there had been 34 cases of mpox reported to the state: 32 in Maricopa County, one in Cochise County and one in Yavapai County, state data shows. "We are monitoring them closely to better understand potential differences between Clade I and II," a news release from the Arizona Department of Health Services says. "Both types of mpox cause similar symptoms and we currently recommend using the same prevention measures including testing, vaccination, clinical management, and public health response." A global outbreak of the less severe Clade II strain of mpox began in 2022 and continues to this day, including in some African countries, according to the World Health Organization. Growing outbreaks of subclades Ia and Ib have also been affecting the Democratic Republic of the Congo and other countries in Africa, the WHO says. Subclade Ib was first detected beyond Africa in 2024, according to the WHO. Symptoms of mpox may include a new or unexplained rash that looks like pimples or blisters and may be painful or itchy. Some people may also experience fever, headache, muscle aches, swollen lymph nodes, chills, exhaustion, or respiratory symptoms, state and federal health officials say, and people with weakened immune systems may be at greater risk for severe illness. Vaccine will help prevent mpox and reduce risk of severe illness Anyone who has had close physical contact with someone infected with mpox has an increased risk of contracting the disease and should get two doses of the JYNNEOS vaccine to both prevent infection and reduce the risk of severe illness. You can get vaccinated after an exposure. Vaccination is most effective when given within four days of exposure but may still reduce illness when given within 14 days, the state health department says. Check for symptoms for 21 days after your last contact. Anyone who develops symptoms should avoid close contact with others, isolate at home and contact a health provider for testing. Individuals who are infected with mpox should stay home and away from other people until all sores have healed, scabs have fallen off and a fresh layer of skin has formed. If you need to be around others, cover rashes or lesions with clothing, gloves or bandages, the state health department says. Other tips for avoiding the spread: Do not have sex or close physical contact if you or your partner has a new or unexplained rash, sores, or other symptoms of mpox. Condoms may reduce exposure in some areas of the body but may not prevent all mpox exposures because sores can appear elsewhere on the body. Consider reducing your number of partners. Other tips for avoiding the spread: Do not have sex or close physical contact if you or your partner has a new or unexplained rash, sores, or other symptoms of mpox. Condoms may reduce exposure in some areas of the body but may not prevent all mpox exposures because sores can appear elsewhere on the body. Consider reducing your number of partners. news.content: U.S. News World News Korea Regional Review Latin America Region Odd News Entertainment Movies Music TV Sports NFL MLB NBA Soccer Voices Photos News US News World News Entertainment Sports Archive Almanac U.S. News July 23, 2026 / 1:28 AM Arizona reports first Clade I mpox case in resident with recent travel By Darryl Coote July 23 (UPI) -- Arizona health officials have confirmed the state's first infection of an mpox strain responsible for a global outbreak, identifying the case as having been infected while traveling outside the United States. The Arizona Department of Health and Services said in a statement Wednesday that it has confirmed its first case of Clade I mpox, involving a person with recent international travel. "ADHS and local public health officials are working to prevent additional infections through monitoring and follow-ups with people who may have been exposed," the state health agency said. "There is currently no evidence of local transmission connected to this case." Little information about the patient was made public. The ADHS said it was notified of a confirmed travel-associated case of the mpox strain this month. It is the state's 34th case of the disease this year, with all but the most recent patient having contracted Clade II mpox. Mpox is an infection caused by the monkeypox virus, which is spread through physical contact, including direct skin-to-skin contact and sharing of personal items, including bedding, towels and clothing, the ADHS said. The virus has two main clades: Clade I, which is endemic to Central Africa, and Clade II, which is associated with West Africa. According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Clade I was historically reported to have a much higher case-fatality rate than Clade II, though recent data suggest case-fatality rates for both clades are low, especially when medical care is provided. Clade II is the cause of the ongoing mpox outbreak that began in 2022, infecting more than 114,000 people worldwide, including about 37,500 people infected in the United States, CDC statistics show. ADHS statistics show Arizona had 582 mpox infections in 2022, followed by 20 in 2023, 66 in 2024 and 17 last year. Clade I is also responsible for an ongoing mpox outbreak that began in Central Africa in late 2023, and which has since spread internationally, resulting in more than 55,000 confirmed cases, including more than 150 deaths, since January 2024, the CDC said. The United States reported between 1,700 and 2,800 mpox cases a year from 2023 through 2025, though nearly all have been Clade II. The CDC said Clade I cases have increased in frequency in the country since March, with more than 20 cases reported in the United States as of June. news.title_zh: 亚利桑那州报告首例近期旅行过的居民 I 型 猴痘 病例 - upi.com
news.source_body_en: Arizona health officials have confirmed the state's first case of Clade I mpox, involving a resident with recent international travel. This marks the 34th mpox case in Arizona this year, with all previous cases being Clade II. The Arizona Department of Health Services (ADHS) stated there is no evidence of local transmission connected to this case and is working to prevent additional infections through monitoring and follow-ups with potentially exposed individuals. Clade I, endemic to Central Africa, has been responsible for an ongoing global outbreak since late 2023, with over 55,000 confirmed cases and more than 150 deaths reported since January 2024. The U.S. has seen an increase in Clade I cases since March, with over 20 cases reported as of June.
news.content_zh: 亚利桑那州卫生官员已确认该州首例 Clade I 猴痘 病例,涉及一名最近有国际旅行经历的居民。这是亚利桑那州今年第 34 起 猴痘 案件,之前的所有案件都是 Clade II。亚利桑那州卫生服务部 (ADHS) 表示,没有证据表明当地 传播 与此病例有关,并正在努力通过监测和跟踪可能暴露的个人来防止更多感染。中非特有的 I 型分支自 2023 年底以来一直是全球 暴发 的罪魁祸首,自 2024 年 1 月以来已报告了 55,000 多例确诊病例和 150 多人死亡。自 3 月份以来,美国的 I 型分支病例有所增加,截至 6 月报告了 20 多例病例。

news.content: Benue Probes Suspected Mpox Case, Urges Residents to Remain Calm By Damilola Olufemi 1 min read File image: A man with Mpox The Benue State Government has commenced an investigation into a suspected case of Mpox reported in Konshisha Local Government Area, saying no outbreak has been confirmed in the state. The state Commissioner for Health and Human Services, Dr Paul Ogwuche, disclosed this on Saturday while responding to reports of a suspected case at the Tyokula Achihi residence in Korinya, Konshisha Local Government Area. According to him, the Director of Public Health was directed to liaise with the State Epidemiologist, who in turn immediately deployed the Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer (DSNO) for Konshisha Local Government Area to the reported location for on-the-ground assessment, case investigation and collection of appropriate clinical samples for laboratory testing. “At this stage, no Mpox outbreak has been confirmed in Benue State. It is important to emphasise that skin rashes and fever can result from several medical conditions, and laboratory confirmation is required before any diagnosis of Mpox can be made,” he said. The commissioner noted that the state’s disease surveillance system remains active across all 23 local government areas. According to him, the ministry is collaborating with the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), the Federal Ministry of Health, the World Health Organisation (WHO) and other development partners to ensure early detection and prompt response to public health threats. He called on residents to remain calm and avoid spreading unverified information that could cause unnecessary panic. “We encourage anyone experiencing fever accompanied by unexplained rashes or blisters to report immediately to the nearest health facility for proper medical evaluation and to avoid close physical contact until assessed by healthcare professionals,” he said. What is Mpox? Mpox is an infectious disease caused by the monkeypox virus. It spreads through close skin-to-skin contact, sexual activity, or touching contaminated items like bedding and towels. Symptoms include a painful rash, swollen lymph nodes, and fever. Most people recover fully within 2 to 4 weeks

news.content_title: FDA Authorizes First Multiplex PCR Assay for HSV, VZV, and Mpox Skin Lesions
news.content: The FDA has granted EUA for the Allplex HSV-1&2/VZV/MPXV Assay (Seegene USA), the first multiplex PCR test designed to simultaneously differentiate HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, and mpox virus from ulcerative skin lesions in a single run. According to a new announcement from Seegene, Inc, the FDA has granted Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) for its Allplex HSV-1&2/VZV/MPXV Assay, described as the first multiplex PCR test designed to support differential diagnosis of viral causes of ulcerative skin lesions in the US market, with the ability to simultaneously detect and differentiate herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), varicella-zoster virus (VZV), and mpox virus (MPXV clades I/II and clade II) from a single clinical sample. 1 HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, and MPXV all produce vesicular, pustular, or ulcerative skin lesions with overlapping clinical presentations, making visual differentiation unreliable. Single-pathogen molecular testing requires separate orders and samples for each suspected pathogen, creating a diagnostic gap when the causative virus is not among those targeted. The EUA positions the Allplex assay as a solution for clinicians encountering undifferentiated skin lesion presentations in settings where mpox, genital herpes, and herpes zoster may be in the differential. “Seegene’s high-multiplex PCR technologies have been widely utilized across global markets,” Jun Kim, CEO of Seegene USA, said in a statement. 1 “This authorization marks an important step in bringing those capabilities more fully into the US market through Seegene USA, enabling the development of locally relevant multiplex diagnostic products.” The Allplex HSV-1&2/VZV/MPXV Assay was developed end-to-end at Seegene USA using three proprietary high-multiplex PCR technologies: Dual Priming Oligonucleotide (DPO), which improves specificity in complex multiplex reactions; Tagging Oligonucleotide Cleavage and Extension (TOCE), which enables simultaneous detection of multiple targets at distinct temperature channels; and Multiple Detection Temperatures (MuDT), which allows individual analyte identification within a single fluorescence channel. 1 The assay was built using Seegene's automated Seegene Digitalized Development System platform, designed to maintain sensitivity and specificity across high-multiplex configurations. What is the Allplex HSV-1&2/VZV/MPXV Assay authorized for? The Allplex HSV-1&2/VZV/MPXV Assay (Seegene USA) received FDA Emergency Use Authorization for simultaneous detection and differentiation of HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, and mpox virus (MPXV clades I/II and clade II) from vesicular, pustular, or ulcerative skin lesion samples in a single PCR reaction. Why is multiplex testing for skin lesion pathogens clinically important? HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, and mpox virus all cause overlapping vesicular or ulcerative skin presentations. Single-pathogen testing misses cases where the causative virus is not among those ordered; a poster at the 2024 Clinical Virology Symposium found the multiplex approach detected HSV, VZV, or MPXV in 54 of 966 samples previously negative by single-target methods. No. The Allplex HSV-1&2/VZV/MPXV Assay received an Emergency Use Authorization, not traditional FDA approval. Clinicians and laboratory directors should review the FDA EUA summary and the assay’s instructions for use for full analytical performance data before clinical implementation. In a poster presented at the 2024 Clinical Virology Symposium, researchers evaluated 966 samples previously reported as negative by single-pathogen molecular testing methods. 1 The multiplex PCR approach identified HSV, VZV, or MPXV clade I/II in 54 of those 966 samples, a 5.6% rate of detection in specimens considered negative by the existing testing paradigm, underscoring the diagnostic gap created by single-target testing. The authorization is clinically relevant against the backdrop of ongoing mpox transmission in the United States . MPXV clade IIb has circulated in the US since the 2022 global outbreak, and clade I has been documented in travelers and sporadic domestic cases in subsequent years. 2 The clinical overlap between mpox lesions and HSV or VZV reactivation is a documented source of misdiagnosis, particularly in HIV-positive patients and other immunocompromised individuals where all three infections carry significant morbidity. For infection preventionists and ID clinicians managing patients with ulcerative genital or cutaneous lesions, the assay's ability to simultaneously rule in or rule out HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, and MPXV in a single run addresses a workflow inefficiency with direct clinical and public health consequences. 1 A patient presenting with a vesiculopustular rash currently requires sequential testing with separate collection swabs and test orders if the treating clinician suspects more than one viral etiology. news.content_original: The FDA has granted EUA for the Allplex HSV-1&2/VZV/MPXV Assay (Seegene USA), the first multiplex PCR test designed to simultaneously differentiate HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, and mpox virus from ulcerative skin lesions in a single run. According to a new announcement from Seegene, Inc, the FDA has granted Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) for its Allplex HSV-1&2/VZV/MPXV Assay, described as the first multiplex PCR test designed to support differential diagnosis of viral causes of ulcerative skin lesions in the US market, with the ability to simultaneously detect and differentiate herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), varicella-zoster virus (VZV), and mpox virus (MPXV clades I/II and clade II) from a single clinical sample. 1 HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, and MPXV all produce vesicular, pustular, or ulcerative skin lesions with overlapping clinical presentations, making visual differentiation unreliable. Single-pathogen molecular testing requires separate orders and samples for each suspected pathogen, creating a diagnostic gap when the causative virus is not among those targeted. The EUA positions the Allplex assay as a solution for clinicians encountering undifferentiated skin lesion presentations in settings where mpox, genital herpes, and herpes zoster may be in the differential. “Seegene’s high-multiplex PCR technologies have been widely utilized across global markets,” Jun Kim, CEO of Seegene USA, said in a statement. 1 “This authorization marks an important step in bringing those capabilities more fully into the US market through Seegene USA, enabling the development of locally relevant multiplex diagnostic products.” The Allplex HSV-1&2/VZV/MPXV Assay was developed end-to-end at Seegene USA using three proprietary high-multiplex PCR technologies: Dual Priming Oligonucleotide (DPO), which improves specificity in complex multiplex reactions; Tagging Oligonucleotide Cleavage and Extension (TOCE), which enables simultaneous detection of multiple targets at distinct temperature channels; and Multiple Detection Temperatures (MuDT), which allows individual analyte identification within a single fluorescence channel. 1 The assay was built using Seegene's automated Seegene Digitalized Development System platform, designed to maintain sensitivity and specificity across high-multiplex configurations. What is the Allplex HSV-1&2/VZV/MPXV Assay authorized for? The Allplex HSV-1&2/VZV/MPXV Assay (Seegene USA) received FDA Emergency Use Authorization for simultaneous detection and differentiation of HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, and mpox virus (MPXV clades I/II and clade II) from vesicular, pustular, or ulcerative skin lesion samples in a single PCR reaction. Why is multiplex testing for skin lesion pathogens clinically important? HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, and mpox virus all cause overlapping vesicular or ulcerative skin presentations. Single-pathogen testing misses cases where the causative virus is not among those ordered; a poster at the 2024 Clinical Virology Symposium found the multiplex approach detected HSV, VZV, or MPXV in 54 of 966 samples previously negative by single-target methods. No. The Allplex HSV-1&2/VZV/MPXV Assay received an Emergency Use Authorization, not traditional FDA approval. Clinicians and laboratory directors should review the FDA EUA summary and the assay’s instructions for use for full analytical performance data before clinical implementation. In a poster presented at the 2024 Clinical Virology Symposium, researchers evaluated 966 samples previously reported as negative by single-pathogen molecular testing methods. 1 The multiplex PCR approach identified HSV, VZV, or MPXV clade I/II in 54 of those 966 samples, a 5.6% rate of detection in specimens considered negative by the existing testing paradigm, underscoring the diagnostic gap created by single-target testing. The authorization is clinically relevant against the backdrop of ongoing mpox transmission in the United States . MPXV clade IIb has circulated in the US since the 2022 global outbreak, and clade I has been documented in travelers and sporadic domestic cases in subsequent years. 2 The clinical overlap between mpox lesions and HSV or VZV reactivation is a documented source of misdiagnosis, particularly in HIV-positive patients and other immunocompromised individuals where all three infections carry significant morbidity. For infection preventionists and ID clinicians managing patients with ulcerative genital or cutaneous lesions, the assay's ability to simultaneously rule in or rule out HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, and MPXV in a single run addresses a workflow inefficiency with direct clinical and public health consequences. 1 A patient presenting with a vesiculopustular rash currently requires sequential testing with separate collection swabs and test orders if the treating clinician suspects more than one viral etiology. Single-tube multiplex testing compresses process and may accelerate isolation decisions, antiviral initiation, and contact notification. Sensitivity and specificity data from the EUA validation studies were not disclosed in the press release. Clinicians and laboratory directors should consult the FDA EUA summary and the Allplex assay’s instructions for use for analytical performance characteristics before clinical implementation. news.title_original: FDA Authorizes First Multiplex PCR Assay for HSV, VZV, and Mpox Skin Lesions - Contagion Live

analysis.time: Published on 2026-07-22. Event date not specified in the evidence.
analysis.location_and_population: Affected population: patients with vesicular, pustular, or ulcerative skin lesions, particularly those with suspected mpox, genital herpes, or herpes zoster.
analysis.event: The FDA granted Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) for the Allplex HSV-1&2/VZV/MPXV Assay (Seegene USA), the first multiplex PCR test designed to simultaneously differentiate HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, and mpox virus from skin lesions in a single run. This is a confirmed regulatory authorization.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: No case counts or deaths reported. The assay addresses a diagnostic gap, as a 2024 study found it detected HSV, VZV, or MPXV in 54 of 966 samples previously negative by single-target methods (5.6% detection rate). Risk level not explicitly stated.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The EUA positions the assay as a solution for undifferentiated skin lesions. Sensitivity and specificity data were not disclosed in the press release. Clinicians are advised to review the FDA EUA summary and assay instructions for use before implementation. The authorization is relevant amid ongoing mpox transmission in the US, with MPXV clade IIb circulating since 2022 and clade I documented in travelers and sporadic cases.

analysis.brief_en: The FDA has authorized the first multiplex PCR assay for simultaneous detection of HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, and mpox virus from skin lesions, addressing a critical diagnostic gap. The Allplex HSV-1&2/VZV/MPXV Assay (Seegene USA) received Emergency Use Authorization, enabling clinicians to differentiate these viruses in a single test run. This is particularly important given the overlapping clinical presentations of these pathogens and the ongoing mpox transmission in the US. A 2024 study demonstrated the assay's value by detecting one of these viruses in 5.6% of samples previously negative by single-target methods. While the authorization streamlines testing and may accelerate treatment decisions, sensitivity and specificity data were not disclosed, requiring clinicians to review the full EUA documentation before implementation.

ExposuresBy Taylor JohnsonPublished on July 23, 2026Source:US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Arizona health officials say a traveler has brought a more worrisome form of mpox into the state, confirming Wednesday that a resident tested positive for clade I, a genetic strain public health experts have linked to more severe illness. The case appears tied to international travel, and the Arizona Department of Health Services reports there is currently no sign the virus is spreading locally. State teams are tracing contacts and working with clinicians to identify anyone who may have been exposed and to offer testing or vaccination when appropriate. In a statement to FOX 10 Phoenix, the department said the diagnosis was confirmed on July 22 and that the patient "acquired the infection while traveling outside the country." Officials told the outlet that investigators have not found evidence of local transmission linked to this case and that they are following standard contact tracing protocols in coordination with local health jurisdictions. Clade I, formerly known as the Congo Basin clade, has historically been associated with more severe disease than clade II, with reported case fatality ratios in some series roughly between 1% and 10%, according to the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. That analysis also notes that vaccines and treatments used in the United States, including the two dose JYNNEOS vaccine, are expected to provide protection against multiple clades, although clinicians are encouraged to test for and document clade information whenever possible. What health officials recommend Health officials advise that anyone who might have been exposed to mpox contact a healthcare provider or local health department so they can be evaluated for testing and post exposure vaccination. The CDC recommends that JYNNEOS be given as soon as possible after exposure, ideally within four days for the best chance to prevent illness, and notes that vaccination up to 14 days after exposure may still help reduce how severe the disease becomes. Local context and next steps The Arizona Department of Health Services told FOX 10 Phoenix that the state has logged 34 mpox cases so far this year as of July 21. Officials said the newly confirmed clade I infection will trigger heightened surveillance, even as they stress that the overall risk to the general public remains low. Public health leaders continue to urge vaccination for people at higher risk and prompt testing for anyone who develops symptoms. People who recently traveled to a country with ongoing clade I transmission, or who develop possible mpox symptoms such as fever, swollen lymph nodes, rectal pain or a blistering rash, are urged to contact a healthcare provider and avoid close physical contact until they have been evaluated. ExposuresBy Taylor JohnsonPublished on July 23, 2026Source:US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Arizona health officials say a traveler has brought a more worrisome form of mpox into the state, confirming Wednesday that a resident tested positive for clade I, a genetic strain public health experts have linked to more severe illness. The case appears tied to international travel, and the Arizona Department of Health Services reports there is currently no sign the virus is spreading locally. State teams are tracing contacts and working with clinicians to identify anyone who may have been exposed and to offer testing or vaccination when appropriate. In a statement to FOX 10 Phoenix, the department said the diagnosis was confirmed on July 22 and that the patient "acquired the infection while traveling outside the country." Officials told the outlet that investigators have not found evidence of local transmission linked to this case and that they are following standard contact tracing protocols in coordination with local health jurisdictions. Clade I, formerly known as the Congo Basin clade, has historically been associated with more severe disease than clade II, with reported case fatality ratios in some series roughly between 1% and 10%, according to the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. That analysis also notes that vaccines and treatments used in the United States, including the two dose JYNNEOS vaccine, are expected to provide protection against multiple clades, although clinicians are encouraged to test for and document clade information whenever possible. What health officials recommend Health officials advise that anyone who might have been exposed to mpox contact a healthcare provider or local health department so they can be evaluated for testing and post exposure vaccination. The CDC recommends that JYNNEOS be given as soon as possible after exposure, ideally within four days for the best chance to prevent illness, and notes that vaccination up to 14 days after exposure may still help reduce how severe the disease becomes. Local context and next steps The Arizona Department of Health Services told FOX 10 Phoenix that the state has logged 34 mpox cases so far this year as of July 21. Officials said the newly confirmed clade I infection will trigger heightened surveillance, even as they stress that the overall risk to the general public remains low. Public health leaders continue to urge vaccination for people at higher risk and prompt testing for anyone who develops symptoms. People who recently traveled to a country with ongoing clade I transmission, or who develop possible mpox symptoms such as fever, swollen lymph nodes, rectal pain or a blistering rash, are urged to contact a healthcare provider and avoid close physical contact until they have been evaluated. No evidence suggests local transmission linked to this case, according to ADHS.Two distinct types of mpox exist: Clade I and Clade II. Arizona has documented Clade II mpox cases spreading throughout the state and nation since 2022.ADHS issued alerts to healthcare providers regarding rising mpox cases reported this summer. Through July 21, 2026, Arizona documented 34 mpox cases combining both Clade I and II variants.Clade I cases typically occur in African regions and remain uncommon in the United States. Officials are closely monitoring these cases to identify potential differences between the two clades.Both mpox types produce similar symptoms, and health authorities currently recommend identical prevention measures. These include testing, vaccination, clinical management, and public health response protocols.The monkeypox virus causes mpox infection, primarily spreading through close personal contact with infected individuals, according to ADHS. Transmission occurs through direct skin-to-skin contact with rashes, sores, scabs or body fluids, as well as through close physical contact.Sharing bedding, towels, clothing, or personal items can spread the virus. Prolonged close contact with infected individuals poses transmission risk, and pregnant individuals can pass the infection to their babies.Casual encounters in stores, offices or airplanes are unlikely to spread mpox, according to health officials.Symptoms include new or unexplained rashes resembling pimples or blisters that may cause pain or itching. Additional symptoms can include fever, headache, muscle aches, swollen lymph nodes, chills, exhaustion, or respiratory issues.Individuals with compromised immune systems face greater risk for severe illness. The JYNNEOS vaccine can prevent mpox and reduce severe illness risk, with two doses providing optimal protection, ADHS said.People recently exposed to infected individuals should contact healthcare providers or local health departments immediately. Post-exposure vaccination works most effectively within four days but may still reduce illness severity when administered within 14 days.Exposed individuals should monitor for symptoms for 21 days following their last contact. Anyone developing symptoms should avoid close contact with others, isolate at home and contact healthcare providers for testing.Infected individuals must remain home and away from others until all sores heal, scabs fall off and fresh skin forms. Rashes or lesions should be covered with clothing, gloves or bandages if proximity to others becomes necessary.Health officials advise against skin-to-skin contact and sharing bedding, towels, clothing, or personal items with symptomatic or diagnosed individuals. Sexual transmission remains possible, and individuals should avoid sex or close physical contact if either partner shows new rashes, sores or other mpox symptoms.Condoms may reduce exposure in some body areas but cannot prevent all mpox exposures since sores can appear anywhere on the body, ADHS said. Reducing partner numbers may lower risk.ADHS will continue monitoring mpox activity and providing updates to healthcare providers and public health partners as new information emerges. news.excerpt: The Benue State Ministry of Health and Human Services has launched an investigation into reports of a suspected Mpox outbreak in Korinya, Konshisha Local Government Area, LGA, following a distress ...

news.content: Vanguard News Home News Top Stories E-editions Politics Metro Business Sports Editorial Columns ALLURE Search for: Home News Top Stories E-editions Politics Metro Business Sports Editorial Columns ALLURE Home News E-Editions Politics Metro Business Sports Editorial Columns Allure Home » News » Mpox: Benue investigates suspected cases in Konshisha LG News Follow us on Google July 25, 2026 Mpox: Benue investigates suspected cases in Konshisha LG Layer 1 By Peter Duru The Benue State Ministry of Health and Human Services has launched an investigation into reports of a suspected Mpox outbreak in Korinya, Konshisha Local Government Area, LGA, following a distress call by residents who appealed for urgent government and international intervention over an unidentified skin disease affecting several people in their community. The alarm was raised by residents of Tyokula Achihi Residence, located along Km 2 Vandeikya Road, Korinya, in a public appeal dated July 25, 2026. The residents claimed that several young men and women had developed severe rashes, fever and blister-like lesions covering their faces, chests, backs and other parts of their bodies, raising fears of a possible Mpox outbreak. In the statement signed by Shadrach Mtsor on behalf of the community, the residents said the illness appeared to be spreading rapidly among people living in close quarters, with many of the affected individuals reportedly being residents within the same compound. “We are making a desperate public appeal for immediate medical intervention over a suspected outbreak of M-Pox in our community. Many of the affected persons are staff and residents within the same compound and have no access to proper diagnosis, isolation or treatment. We fear this could spread to the wider Korinya community and beyond if not contained now,” the statement read. The community appealed to the World Health Organization (WHO), the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), the Federal Ministry of Health, the Benue State Ministry of Health and Human Services, the Benue State Emergency Management Agency (BSEMA), UNICEF, the Nigerian Red Cross and Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) to urgently deploy medical personnel to investigate the cases. Among the interventions requested were the immediate deployment of a rapid response medical team to assess and test the suspected cases, provision of isolation materials, personal protective equipment and hygiene kits, free medical treatment for affected persons, public health education to prevent further transmission, and possible temporary closure and decontamination of the affected workplace if necessary. “Our community is poor and cannot handle this alone. The victims are isolated in their rooms without medical care. We are scared. We appeal to all well-meaning bodies, NGOs and government agencies to come to our aid before this becomes a bigger epidemic,” the residents added. Responding to the reports, the Commissioner for Health and Human Services, Dr. Paul Ogwuche, said the Ministry had immediately activated its disease surveillance system in line with established public health protocols after becoming aware of the reports circulating on social media. According to the Commissioner, the Director of Public Health was instructed to work with the State Epidemiologist, who promptly deployed the Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer (DSNO) for Konshisha LGA to the affected community to conduct an on-the-ground assessment, investigate the suspected cases and collect clinical samples for laboratory analysis. Dr. Ogwuche, however, stressed that no Mpox outbreak had been confirmed in Benue State, noting that laboratory testing remained the only basis for confirming the disease.Related NewsFresh attacks rock Benue's Sankera axis; one killedLassa fever death toll hits 229 as fresh infections riseLassa fever death toll hits 229 as fresh infections rise “At this stage, no Mpox outbreak has been confirmed in Benue State. It is important to emphasise that skin rashes and fever can result from several medical conditions, and laboratory confirmation is required before any diagnosis of Mpox can be made,” he stated. The commissioner assured residents that the administration of Governor Hyacinth Alia remained committed to protecting public health, adding that disease surveillance remained active across all 23 LGA of the state in collaboration with the NCDC, the Federal Ministry of Health, the WHO and other development partners. He urged members of the public to remain calm and refrain from spreading unverified information capable of causing unnecessary panic, while encouraging anyone experiencing fever accompanied by unexplained rashes or blisters to report immediately to the nearest health facility for proper medical evaluation and to avoid close physical contact until assessed by healthcare professionals. Dr. Ogwuche also commended members of the Korinya community for promptly reporting the suspected cases, describing early reporting as critical to effective disease surveillance and emergency response. He assured that the Ministry would make the findings of the investigation public as soon as laboratory results become available, adding that appropriate response measures would be implemented immediately in accordance with national public health guidelines if the suspected cases were confirmed to be Mpox or any other disease of public health concern. news.content: Discover morenewsHistoryAfricans & DiasporaSkin ConditionsHealthOBGYNGovernmentpublic healthGeographic ReferenceHealth Conditions ▼ × ×search Advertise with us Sunday, July 26, 2026 Most Widely Read Newspaper Subscribe: Punch E-Paper Subscribe: Punch E-Paper Home News Featured 2026 World Cup Metro Plus Business Sports HealthWise Editorial Columns Videos Continuation From Print PunchNG Menu: Politics Spice Special Features Education Sex & Relationship Interview Columns Opinion Advertise with us Benue probes suspected Mpox case July 26, 2026 12:24 am Photo Credit: Women health mag By John Charles Kindly share this story: The Benue State Commissioner of Health and Human Services, Dr Paul Ogwuche, has urged residents to remain calm over a suspected case of Monkeypox in Konshisha Local Government Area, saying the ministry is investigating the reported case. The commissioner was responding to the alleged suspected case of Mpox reported to have been discovered at Tyokula Achihi residence, in the local government. According to him, the ministry immediately activated its surveillance system in line with established public health protocols and visited the area. Ogwuche, who disclosed this in a statement on Saturday, noted that the public should not jump to conclusions whenever skin rashes and fever surface. He added that such symptoms could result from several medical conditions, stressing that laboratory confirmation is required before any diagnosis of Mpox can be made. Related News Suspected armed herders kill three in fresh Benue attacks Benue investigates suspected Mpox case IG did not issue ‘shoot-on-sight’ order in Benue — Police The statement read partly, “The Director of Public Health was directed to liaise with the state Epidemiologist, who in turn immediately deployed the Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer (DSNO) for Konshisha Local Government Area to the reported location for on-the-ground assessment, case investigation and collection of appropriate clinical samples for laboratory testing. “At this stage, no Mpox outbreak has been confirmed in Benue State. It is important to emphasise that skin rashes and fever can result from several medical conditions, and laboratory confirmation is required before any diagnosis of Mpox can be made.” The commissioner said the state disease surveillance system remained active across all 23 local government areas, adding that the ministry maintained close collaboration with the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention, the Federal Ministry of Health, the World Health Organisation and other development partners to ensure prompt detection and response to any public health event. Ogwuche appealed to members of the public to remain calm and avoid spreading unverified information capable of creating unnecessary panic. “We encourage anyone experiencing fever accompanied by unexplained rashes or blisters to report immediately to the nearest health facility for proper medical evaluation and to avoid close physical contact until assessed by healthcare professionals,” the statement read in part. BY KYLIE WERNER Jul 22, 2026, 8:59 PM 1 Follow on Google News Watch: BREAKING: U.S. Sen. Ruben Gallego says he’s considering running for president on KTAR | 22 mins The Arizona Department of Health Services (ADHS) confirmed the first case of Clade I mpox in Arizona on Wednesday. There are two types of mpox, Clade I and Clade II, and as of Tuesday 34 cases have been reported in the state between the two this year. In fact, there have been cases of Clade II mpox spreading in Arizona and the U.S. since 2022. The department is monitoring them to try and understand the difference between the two types as they have similar symptoms and the same prevention measures are recommended for both. ADVERTISEMENT ADHS was notified this month that a resident contracted the infection while traveling outside the country. The department and public health officials are doing their part to prevent spread of the virus by doing follow-ups with people potentially exposed. It noted that there is currently no indication of local transmission connected to the case. ADHS said that Clade I cases are typically found in parts of Africa and are less common in the U.S. What are the symptoms of Mpox? Mpox is caused by the monkeypox virus and spread through close contact with someone who is infected. That includes skin-to-skin contact with rash, sores, scabs or bodily fluids as well as sharing bedding, towels, clothing or other items. It was also noted that mpox can be passed during pregnancy to a baby. ADHS highlighted that the infection is unlikely to spread through casual contact at stores, offices or on airplanes. One of the symptoms of mpox is a rash that looks like pimples or blisters, which can be painful or itchy. There are some who also get a fever, headache, muscles aches, swollen lymph nodes, chills, exhaustion or respiratory symptoms. It was advised that people who believe they are at risk get the JYNNEOS vaccine, which requires two doses for the best protection. The vaccine is most effective within four days of exposure, but might still reduce the infection when received within 14 days. Those who are exposed should contact a healthcare provider or local health department, get tested and check for symptoms for 21 days after the contact. People who develop symptoms are also advised to isolate at home and avoid close contact with others. Those who test positive for mpox are told to isolate at home and stay away from people until their sores have healed, scabs have fallen off and there is a fresh layer of skin. People who are infected that have to be around others should cover their rashes or lesions with clothing, gloves or bandages. analysis_en.location_and_population: Arizona, USA; a resident who contracted the infection while traveling outside the country.
analysis_en.event: The Arizona Department of Health Services (ADHS) confirmed the first case of Clade I mpox in Arizona. The case is travel-related, and there is no indication of local transmission.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: As of Tuesday, 34 mpox cases (both Clade I and Clade II) have been reported in Arizona this year. ADHS states the public risk is low.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: ADHS is monitoring cases to understand the difference between Clade I and Clade II. Follow-ups are being conducted with potentially exposed individuals. No local transmission has been detected. The department recommends the JYNNEOS vaccine for at-risk individuals and advises isolation for those infected.

Health authorities recommend preventive measures, including vaccination with the JYNNEOS vaccine for those at risk, and advise isolation for infected individuals until symptoms fully resolve.

news.content_title: Arizona Department of Health Services confirms Arizona's first travel-associated Clade I Mpox case; public risk remains low
news.content: Arizona health officials have confirmed the state's first travel-related case of Clade I mpox, a strain of the virus more commonly found in parts of Africa, according to the Arizona Department of Health Services. The infected Arizona resident contracted the virus while traveling outside the United States. ADHS said there is currently no evidence the case has led to local transmission in Arizona, and the overall risk to the general public remains low. State and local health officials are conducting contact tracing and monitoring individuals who may have been exposed to help prevent additional infections. Mpox is caused by the monkeypox virus and spreads primarily through close, personal contact. Health officials say transmission can occur through direct contact with a rash, sores, or bodily fluids, as well as through shared bedding, towels, clothing, and prolonged close contact with an infected person. Casual interactions in public places such as stores, offices, or airplanes are considered unlikely to spread the virus. Arizona has reported 34 mpox cases so far in 2026, including both Clade I and Clade II infections. Clade II has been circulating in Arizona and across the United States since 2022, while Clade I cases remain uncommon in the U.S. According to ADHS, symptoms of mpox include a new or unexplained rash that may appear as pimples or blisters, along with fever, headache, muscle aches, swollen lymph nodes, chills, exhaustion, and respiratory symptoms. People with weakened immune systems may face a higher risk of severe illness. Health officials continue to recommend vaccination for people at increased risk of exposure. The two-dose JYNNEOS vaccine can help prevent mpox and reduce the severity of illness. Anyone who develops symptoms should avoid close contact with others, isolate at home, and contact a healthcare provider for testing. ADHS officials say they will continue monitoring mpox activity statewide and provide updates as new information becomes available. news.content: Home News Politics Metro Sport Entertainment Opinion Education Health Interview Daily Post Ghana Connect with us Daily Post Nigeria ‘No confirmed Mpox case in Benue’ – Health Commissioner Home News Politics Metro Entertainment Sport Health ‘No confirmed Mpox case in Benue’ – Health Commissioner Published on July 25, 2026 By Ejembi Ogwuche The Benue State Ministry of Health and Human Services has dismissed rumours making the rounds that there is a reported case of monkeypox in the state. This was contained in a statement on Saturday by the Commissioner for Health and Human Services, Dr Paul Ogwuche. He said the ministry had become aware of reports circulating on social media regarding a suspected Mpox outbreak at Tyokula Achihi Residence, Korinya, Konshisha Local Government Area. Dr Ogwuche said immediately the information came to the ministry’s attention, it activated its surveillance system in line with established public health protocols. According to him, “The Director of Public Health was directed to liaise with the State Epidemiologist, who in turn immediately deployed the Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer (DSNO) for Konshisha Local Government Area to the reported location for on-the-ground assessment, case investigation and collection of appropriate clinical samples for laboratory testing.” He said that, at this stage, no Mpox outbreak had been confirmed in Benue State. “It is important to emphasise that skin rashes and fever can result from several medical conditions, and laboratory confirmation is required before any diagnosis of Mpox can be made,” he said. Dr Ogwuche said further, “Our disease surveillance system remains active across all 23 Local Government Areas, and we maintain close collaboration with the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), the Federal Ministry of Health, the World Health Organization (WHO), and other development partners to ensure prompt detection and response to any public health event.” The commissioner appealed to members of the public to remain calm and avoid spreading unverified information capable of creating unnecessary panic. “We encourage anyone experiencing fever accompanied by unexplained rashes or blisters to report immediately to the nearest health facility for proper medical evaluation and to avoid close physical contact until assessed by healthcare professionals. “We commend members of the community for promptly reporting the situation, as early reporting is essential for effective disease surveillance and response,” he stated. “Should the results confirm Mpox or any other disease of public health importance, appropriate response measures will be implemented immediately in accordance with national guidelines,” he added. news.content_title: Benue begins probe into suspected Mpox case
news.content: Stay connected via Google News The Benue ministry of health says it has commenced an investigation into reports of a suspected Mpox case in Konshisha LGA of the state. In a statement issued on Saturday, Paul Ogwuche, commissioner of health, said no outbreak has been confirmed in the state. Ogwuche said the ministry has activated its disease surveillance system after reports circulating on social media alleged a suspected Mpox outbreak at Tyokula Achihi in Konshisha LGA. Ogwuche said the director of public health had directed the state epidemiologist to deploy the disease surveillance and notification officer (DSNO) for Konshisha to conduct an on-the-ground assessment, investigate the suspected case and collect clinical samples for laboratory testing. Advertisement He cautioned that laboratory analysis is required before Mpox can be confirmed, noting that fever and skin rashes may be symptoms of several medical conditions. “Our disease surveillance system remains active across all 23 LGAs, and we maintain close collaboration with the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), the Federal Ministry of Health, the World Health Organization (WHO), and other development partners to ensure prompt detection and response to any public health event,” Ogwuche said. The commissioner urged residents to refrain from spreading unverified information capable of causing unnecessary panic. Advertisement He advised anyone experiencing fever accompanied by unexplained rashes and blisters to seek immediate medical attention at the nearest health facility. “We commend members of the community for promptly reporting the situation, as early reporting is essential for effective disease surveillance and response,” the commissioner said. “The ministry will continue to keep the public informed as soon as the investigation and laboratory findings become available. Should the results confirm Mpox or any other disease of public health importance, appropriate response measures will be implemented immediately in accordance with national guidelines.”

news.content: Discover moreInfectious DiseasesMedical Literature & ResourcesAfricans & DiasporagovernmentPoliticsGovernmentHealthpublic healthGeographic ReferenceNEWS ▼ × ×search Advertise with us Sunday, July 26, 2026 Most Widely Read Newspaper Subscribe: Punch E-Paper Subscribe: Punch E-Paper Home News Featured 2026 World Cup Metro Plus Business Sports HealthWise Editorial Columns Videos Continuation From Print PunchNG Menu: Politics Spice Special Features Education Sex & Relationship Interview Columns Opinion Advertise with us Benue investigates suspected Mpox case July 25, 2026 7:12 pm By John Charles Kindly share this story: The Benue State Government has commenced investigations into a suspected case of Mpox reported in Konshisha Local Government Area of the state. The Commissioner for Health and Human Services, Dr Paul Ogwuche, disclosed this on Saturday while responding to reports of a suspected case at the Tyokula Achihi residence in Korinya, Konshisha LGA. Ogwuche said the ministry immediately activated its surveillance system in line with established public health protocols and deployed officials to the area. In a statement made available to journalists in Makurdi, the commissioner urged residents not to jump to conclusions whenever skin rashes and fever occur, noting that the symptoms could result from several medical conditions. He stressed that laboratory confirmation was required before any case could be diagnosed as Mpox. The statement read in part, “The Director of Public Health was directed to liaise with the State Epidemiologist, who in turn immediately deployed the Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer (DSNO) for Konshisha Local Government Area to the reported location for on-the-ground assessment, case investigation and collection of appropriate clinical samples for laboratory testing. “At this stage, no Mpox outbreak has been confirmed in Benue State. It is important to emphasise that skin rashes and fever can result from several medical conditions, and laboratory confirmation is required before any diagnosis of Mpox can be made.” Related News Stop wasting your destiny, Oyedepo warns youths against betting Matawalle consoles victims of Zamfara terrorist attacks NDLEA arrests Lagos businessman over 3.3kg cocaine bound for UK The commissioner said the state disease surveillance system remained active across all 23 local government areas. He added that the ministry was working closely with the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention, the Federal Ministry of Health, the World Health Organisation and other development partners to ensure prompt detection and response to public health events. Ogwuche urged members of the public to remain calm and avoid spreading unverified information capable of creating unnecessary panic. “We encourage anyone experiencing fever accompanied by unexplained rashes or blisters to report immediately to the nearest health facility for proper medical evaluation and to avoid close physical contact until assessed by healthcare professionals,” the statement added. The commissioner said the ministry would continue to keep the public informed as soon as the investigation and laboratory findings became available. He added that appropriate response measures would be implemented in line with national guidelines if the results confirmed Mpox or any other disease of public health importance. news.content: Support Star Observer Fund Australia’s home of LGBTQIA+ journalism Support Us Subscribe Login Support Star ObserverFund Australia’s home of LGBTQ+ journalism Support Us Subscribe News International National News New South Wales News Victorian News Queensland News Entertainment Movies & TV Celebrity Drag Stage Music Gaming Books The Internet Directory Archives Scene Photos In Print Subscribe Advertise News International National News New South Wales News Victorian News Queensland News Entertainment Movies & TV Celebrity Drag Stage Music Gaming Books The Internet Directory Archives Scene Photos In Print Subscribe Advertise News Entertainment What’s on Trending Directory News Entertainment What’s on Trending Directory About Advertise Scene Photos In Print Contact Terms & Conditions About Advertise Scene Photos In Print Contact Terms & Conditions Search CLEAR Search Authorities Warn Mpox Cases Are On The Rise In Western Australia News Western Australia Michael James July 21, 2026 The Western Australia community is being warned to be on the alert after an increase in cases of Mpox was reported in the state. Authorities from the Department Of Health in Western Australia issued the update overnight. They warn the current cases to day in 2026 have exceeded all of those in 2025. Mpox on the rise in Western Australia According to Western Australia Department Of Health there have been 36 confirmed cases of Mpox in 2026 so far. Comparatively in the whole of 2025 there were just 28 confirmed cases and just 23 cases in 2024 in the state. The government identified that whilst the cases effected both gay and bisexual men as well as heterosexual men and women, the majority of the cases have effected the queer community. “While the majority of cases have been in gay, bisexual and men who have sex with men (GBMSM), several infections have also been identified in heterosexual men and women this year” the government said in a statement overnight. They warned “Western Australians to be aware of the signs and symptoms of mpox and to seek medical advice if they develop symptoms.” Director of the Communicable Disease Control Directorate, Dr Paul Armstrong reminded the public of the importance of safe sex, including the use of condoms, as well as ensuring early testing and getting vaccinated. “While most infections continue to occur in specific higher-risk groups, mpox can affect anyone who has close physical contact with an infected person,” Dr Armstrong said. “It’s important that anyone who develops symptoms, particularly an unexplained rash or skin lesions, seeks medical advice promptly and avoids close contact with others until they have been assessed.” “We are encouraging people who are eligible for vaccination to ensure they are fully protected by receiving both doses of the vaccine.” “Vaccination is recommended for people at higher risk of exposure, including eligible gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men, sex workers and other people whose sexual practices place them at increased risk of mpox infection. A Medicare Card is not required for a free vaccination.” Earlier this year Thorne Harbour Health in Melbourne warned of a spike of Mpox cases across multiple states in Australia, reporting over 100 confirmed cases nationally. “While our communities have done well to keep mpox cases down, the reality is that it hasn’t disappeared entirely. Unfortunately, this is the time of year when we have seen a spike in cases in both the 2022 and 2024 outbreak,” said Caleb Hawk, THH’s Deputy Director of Health Promotion and Community Engagement at the time. The first confirmed case of Mpox was detected back in May 2022, since then cases have fluctuated, with no cases between November 2022 and May 2023 when two more cases were detected in Sydney. More cases were reported in Victoria in April 2024, with numbers continuing to rise later that year with WHO declaring Mpox a “Global Health Emergency” in August 2024. In July 2025 a second case of a rare strain of the virus was detected in Brisbane, as overall numbers starting to decline the public was still encouraged to continue vaccinations. Mpox vaccinations remain free and available, regardless of Medicare or visa status. For more information about how to get the mpox vaccination, head here. analysis.time: Published on July 21, 2026. Event date refers to the increase in Mpox cases reported in Western Australia in 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Western Australia, Australia. The affected population includes gay, bisexual, and men who have sex with men (GBMSM), as well as heterosexual men and women.
analysis.event: Confirmed increase in Mpox cases in Western Australia. The Western Australia Department of Health reported that cases in 2026 have exceeded those in 2025 and 2024.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 36 confirmed cases in 2026 compared to 28 in 2025 and 23 in 2024. The majority of cases have affected the queer community, but infections have also been identified in heterosexual men and women. No explicit risk level is stated.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Authorities are advising the public to seek medical advice if symptoms develop, practice safe sex, and get vaccinated. Vaccination is free and available regardless of Medicare or visa status. The public is encouraged to receive both doses of the vaccine.

analysis.brief_en: Western Australian authorities are warning of a rise in Mpox cases, with 36 confirmed cases in 2026 already surpassing the 28 cases reported in all of 2025. The majority of cases have affected the queer community, particularly gay, bisexual, and men who have sex with men, though infections have also been identified in heterosexual men and women. The Western Australia Department of Health is urging residents to recognize symptoms, seek medical advice promptly, and practice safe sex. Free Mpox vaccinations are available to eligible higher-risk groups, including GBMSM, sex workers, and others with increased exposure risk. The public is encouraged to ensure they are fully vaccinated with both doses.

“畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接Article Open access 摘要猴痘在多国的暴发促使世界卫生组织将其宣布为国际关注的公共卫生紧急事件。鉴于尼日利亚近期出现的病例以及医学生可能面临的风险,本研究调查了尼日利亚西北部医学生对猴痘疫苗的认知、态度、接受度及支付意愿。研究在尼日利亚西北部的卡诺州贝约大学和卡杜纳州扎里亚的艾哈迈杜·贝洛大学,对100级至600级的医学生进行了横断面调查。通过便利抽样方法共获得了301份回复。数据通过在线自填问卷收集,其中包括6项社会人口学资料、5项关于认知的题目、6项关于态度的题目、5项关于接受度的题目,以及6项关于支付意愿的题目。数据以频率和百分比的形式呈现。研究采用卡方检验和二元逻辑回归分析影响支付意愿的因素。共有301名医学生参与了这项研究。其中大多数人的年龄在21至25岁之间(n?=?176,58.6%),性别为男性(n?=?199,66.1%)。贝约大学贡献了最多的受访者(n?=?184,61.1%),而300级的学生占比最低(n?=?25,8.3%)。在宗教和种族方面,大多数参与者为穆斯林(n?=?262,87.0%)和豪萨人(n?=?168,55.8%)。在301名受访者中,203人(67.4%,95%置信区间:62.1%?72.6%)了解猴痘疫苗,95人(31.6%)对接种疫苗持积极态度。疫苗的接受度很高,有245人(81.4%,95%置信区间:77%?85.6%)愿意接种该疫苗。疫苗的支付意愿与年龄组(χ2 (3)?=?13.839,p?=?0.003)和学习阶段(χ2 (5)?=?15.603,p?=?0.008)存在显著关联。二元逻辑回归分析出三个影响支付意愿的独立因素:对疫苗可负担性和可获得性的认知(AOR?=?0.379,95%置信区间:0.204–0.704,p?=?0.002)、对疫苗重要性的认知(AOR?=?0.444,95%置信区间:0.275–0.719,p?=?0.001),以及对副作用的担忧(AOR?=?0.489,95%置信区间:0.244–0.979,p?=?0.043)。尽管疫苗的接受度很高,但经济障碍仍是尼日利亚西北部医学生接种猴痘疫苗面临的主要问题。当疫苗广泛可用时,需要采取针对可负担性、疫苗知识普及和安全信息传递的干预措施,以提高人们的支付意愿并促进疫苗的接种。欢迎下载最佳的病毒清除验证和细胞库检测方案>>>领 取 打赏 展开全文 开通VIP 享海量文章 全站开放获取+解锁超过 200万篇新闻全文+每日更新 2000+篇,学术前沿动态全时追踪! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接Article Open access 摘要猴痘在多国的暴发促使世界卫生组织将其宣布为国际关注的公共卫生紧急事件。鉴于尼日利亚近期出现的病例以及医学生可能面临的风险,本研究调查了尼日利亚西北部医学生对猴痘疫苗的认知、态度、接受度及支付意愿。研究在尼日利亚西北部的卡诺州贝约大学和卡杜纳州扎里亚的艾哈迈杜·贝洛大学,对100级至600级的医学生进行了横断面调查。通过便利抽样方法共获得了301份回复。数据通过在线自填问卷收集,其中包括6项社会人口学资料、5项关于认知的题目、6项关于态度的题目、5项关于接受度的题目,以及6项关于支付意愿的题目。数据以频率和百分比的形式呈现。研究采用卡方检验和二元逻辑回归分析影响支付意愿的因素。共有301名医学生参与了这项研究。其中大多数人的年龄在21至25岁之间(n?=?176,58.6%),性别为男性(n?=?199,66.1%)。贝约大学贡献了最多的受访者(n?=?184,61.1%),而300级的学生占比最低(n?=?25,8.3%)。在宗教和种族方面,大多数参与者为穆斯林(n?=?262,87.0%)和豪萨人(n?=?168,55.8%)。在301名受访者中,203人(67.4%,95%置信区间:62.1%?72.6%)了解猴痘疫苗,95人(31.6%)对接种疫苗持积极态度。疫苗的接受度很高,有245人(81.4%,95%置信区间:77%?85.6%)愿意接种该疫苗。疫苗的支付意愿与年龄组(χ2 (3)?=?13.839,p?=?0.003)和学习阶段(χ2 (5)?=?15.603,p?=?0.008)存在显著关联。二元逻辑回归分析出三个影响支付意愿的独立因素:对疫苗可负担性和可获得性的认知(AOR?=?0.379,95%置信区间:0.204–0.704,p?=?0.002)、对疫苗重要性的认知(AOR?=?0.444,95%置信区间:0.275–0.719,p?=?0.001),以及对副作用的担忧(AOR?=?0.489,95%置信区间:0.244–0.979,p?=?0.043)。尽管疫苗的接受度很高,但经济障碍仍是尼日利亚西北部医学生接种猴痘疫苗面临的主要问题。当疫苗广泛可用时,需要采取针对可负担性、疫苗知识普及和安全信息传递的干预措施,以提高人们的支付意愿并促进疫苗的接种。欢迎下载最佳的病毒清除验证和细胞库检测方案>>>领 取 打赏 展开全文 开通VIP 享海量文章 全站开放获取+解锁超过 200万篇新闻全文+每日更新 2000+篇,学术前沿动态全时追踪! analysis.time: Published on 2026-07-21; Study conducted in Nigeria's northwestern region.
analysis.location_and_population: Nigeria, specifically Kano State (Bayero University) and Kaduna State (Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria); medical students from 100 to 600 level.
analysis.event: A cross-sectional survey investigating mpox vaccine attitudes, acceptability, and willingness to pay among Nigerian medical students; 301 participants responded.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 203 students (67.4%) were aware of mpox vaccine; 95 (31.6%) had positive attitudes; 245 (81.4%) were willing to vaccinate. Economic barriers were the primary issue affecting vaccination willingness.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Study identified key factors influencing payment willingness: affordability/accessibility (AOR=0.379), perceived importance (AOR=0.444), and side effect concerns (AOR=0.489). Interventions targeting affordability, knowledge, and safety information are recommended to improve uptake.

analysis.brief_en: A cross-sectional study published in Scientific Reports on July 21, 2026, investigated mpox vaccine attitudes and acceptability among 301 medical students in northwestern Nigeria. Conducted at Bayero University (Kano) and Ahmadu Bello University (Zaria), the survey found high vaccine acceptability (81.4%) but significant economic barriers. While 67.4% of students were aware of the vaccine, only 31.6% held positive attitudes. Statistical analysis revealed that affordability/accessibility, perceived importance, and side effect concerns independently influenced willingness to pay. The study recommends targeted interventions addressing cost, knowledge gaps, and safety communication to enhance vaccination rates among this high-risk group.

supplementary_news.content: U.S. News World News Korea Regional Review Latin America Region Odd News Entertainment Movies Music TV Sports NFL MLB NBA Soccer Voices Photos News US News World News Entertainment Sports Archive Almanac U.S. News July 23, 2026 / 1:28 AM Arizona reports first Clade I mpox case in resident with recent travel By Darryl Coote July 23 (UPI) -- Arizona health officials have confirmed the state's first infection of an mpox strain responsible for a global outbreak, identifying the case as having been infected while traveling outside the United States. The Arizona Department of Health and Services said in a statement Wednesday that it has confirmed its first case of Clade I mpox, involving a person with recent international travel. "ADHS and local public health officials are working to prevent additional infections through monitoring and follow-ups with people who may have been exposed," the state health agency said. "There is currently no evidence of local transmission connected to this case." Little information about the patient was made public. The ADHS said it was notified of a confirmed travel-associated case of the mpox strain this month. It is the state's 34th case of the disease this year, with all but the most recent patient having contracted Clade II mpox. Mpox is an infection caused by the monkeypox virus, which is spread through physical contact, including direct skin-to-skin contact and sharing of personal items, including bedding, towels and clothing, the ADHS said. The virus has two main clades: Clade I, which is endemic to Central Africa, and Clade II, which is associated with West Africa. According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Clade I was historically reported to have a much higher case-fatality rate than Clade II, though recent data suggest case-fatality rates for both clades are low, especially when medical care is provided. Clade II is the cause of the ongoing mpox outbreak that began in 2022, infecting more than 114,000 people worldwide, including about 37,500 people infected in the United States, CDC statistics show. ADHS statistics show Arizona had 582 mpox infections in 2022, followed by 20 in 2023, 66 in 2024 and 17 last year. Clade I is also responsible for an ongoing mpox outbreak that began in Central Africa in late 2023, and which has since spread internationally, resulting in more than 55,000 confirmed cases, including more than 150 deaths, since January 2024, the CDC said. The United States reported between 1,700 and 2,800 mpox cases a year from 2023 through 2025, though nearly all have been Clade II. The CDC said Clade I cases have increased in frequency in the country since March, with more than 20 cases reported in the United States as of June.
